sentence: Their run reached [[52.3]]\% [47.6, 57.0] top-1 success and 51.2\% \pbvalid{} success, 6.1 points above our baseline (their run succeeded on 49 complexes where ours failed, ours on 23 where theirs failed; exact McNemar $p = 0.003$).
paragraph: The PoseBusters authors also docked these 428 complexes with Vina and released their per-complex results with the dataset . Their run reached 52.3\% [47.6, 57.0] top-1 success and 51.2\% \pbvalid{} success, 6.1 points above our baseline (their run succeeded on 49 complexes where ours failed, ours on 23 where theirs failed; exact McNemar $p = 0.003$). The two runs agreed on 356 of the 428 complexes. Our preparation failures account for little of the difference: their run solved 5 of those 16 complexes, and on the 412 we docked the gap was 5.1 points (53.2\% against 48.1\%, $p = 0.014$). The protocols differ in several of the choices studied here. Theirs used Vina 1.2.3 with exhaustiveness 32 and 40 poses, a cubic search box of side 25 centred on the crystal ligand, and receptors protonated with Reduce and converted with the prepare\_receptor script of ADFR ( , ESI section S1), against exhaustiveness 8, nine poses, a box padded by 4 around the ligand and PDBFixer/OpenMM preparation here. Our 2 -padding arm reached 53.0\%, not significantly different from their result ($p = 0.82$). A difference of six points between two careful Vina protocols on the same complexes is itself comparable

sentence: A pose within 2 was among the nine returned for 303 complexes ([[70.8]]\%), but ranked first for only 198.
paragraph: At the baseline padding, scoring and search limited success about equally. A pose within 2 was among the nine returned for 303 complexes (70.8\%), but ranked first for only 198. Of the 230 complexes without a top-1 success, 105 were scoring failures (a correct pose returned but not ranked first), while 109 had no correct pose among those returned: 89 in the right site in the wrong binding mode and 20 in the wrong site; 16 failed preparation; a further 19 top poses were correct but not \pbvalid{}.

sentence: epeating the Vina baseline with four docking seeds gave top-1 success of [[46.3]]\%, 46.7\%, 47.0\% and 47.2\% (mean 46.8\%, standard deviation 0.4 points, range 0.9 points).
paragraph: Repeating the Vina baseline with four docking seeds gave top-1 success of 46.3\%, 46.7\%, 47.0\% and 47.2\% (mean 46.8\%, standard deviation 0.4 points, range 0.9 points). The aggregate rate is therefore stable to within one point. Individual outcomes are less stable: two seeds disagree on 17.5 complexes on average (16 – 19 across the six pairs). Over the four replicates, 183 complexes always succeeded, 212 always failed and 33 (7.7\%) changed outcome with the seed alone. We use 17.5 changed complexes as a reference level for how many outcomes an arm changes; it is a yardstick, not a significance threshold.

Over the four replicates, 183 complexes always succeeded, 212 always failed and 33 (7.7\%) changed outcome with the seed alone. We use 17.5 changed complexes as a reference level for how many outcomes an arm changes; it is a yardstick, not a significance threshold.

paragraph: [h] \centering {Paired comparison of each arm with the Vina baseline on all 428 complexes (failures counted as failures). Top-1 success with 95\% Wilson interval; $\Delta$ with a 95\% interval for the paired difference (Newcombe); gained and lost are complexes that succeed in only the arm or only the baseline; $p$ is the exact McNemar test, Holm-adjusted over the five arms. Changed: complexes whose outcome differs from the baseline, and the ratio to the 17.5 changed by a change of seed.} \small

sentence: The clearest case is the start conformer: it changed 85 outcomes, [[4.9]] times the seed level, although its net effect was only +4.4 points.
paragraph: Every Vina arm changed the outcome of more complexes than a change of seed did (Table~ , last column), though for the 6 box only just (28 against 16 – 19 between pairs of seeds). The clearest case is the start conformer: it changed 85 outcomes, 4.9 times the seed level, although its net effect was only +4.4 points. These ratios are descriptive: they compare counts of changed outcomes and do not test whether one source of change matters more than the other. Most of these changes cancel, so a small net difference hides a large reshuffling of which complexes succeed. Net success rates alone therefore understate how much a preparation choice matters for any individual complex.

sentence: nina, which searches with the same machinery but re-ranks poses with a convolutional neural network, reached [[62.6]]\% [57.9, 67.1] at baseline, 16.4 points above Vina (103 complexes gained, 33 lost; $p = 1.4 \times 10^{-9}$).
paragraph: Gnina, which searches with the same machinery but re-ranks poses with a convolutional neural network, reached 62.6\% [57.9, 67.1] at baseline, 16.4 points above Vina (103 complexes gained, 33 lost; $p = 1.4 \times 10^{-9}$). The difference is not an artefact of Vina's 16 preparation failures: on the 412 complexes both engines docked, success was 48.1\% for Vina and 63.1\% for Gnina ($p = 3.8 \times 10^{-8}$). No preparation choice changed Gnina's success significantly. The 2 box gave +3.0 points [$-0.5$, 6.5] and the 8 box $-4.0$ points (Holm $p = 0.47$ and $0.30$); ligand protonation gave $-3.3$ points and the RDKit conformer +0.7 points.

paragraph: Removing cofactors affects the PoseBusters checks more than it affects success. Of the 428 complexes, 244 contain a heterogen other than common additives (organic cofactors, metal and other ions). Among them, a correct top pose (RMSD below 2 ) failed PoseBusters only on a cofactor check for 13 complexes with Vina, 12 with Smina, 24 with Gnina and 7 with rDock, poses placed where a removed cofactor would be. On the 184 complexes without such heterogens, baseline top-1 success was 46.7\% for Vina, 47.3\% for Smina, 62.0\% for Gnina and 34.8\% for rDock, so the engines kept their order. The 2 box raised success for all four (Vina +6.5 points [1.2, 11.8]; Smina +7.1 [2.1, 12.0]; Gnina +2.2 [$-2.8$, 7.1]; rDock +9.2 [3.4, 14.9]), significantly after correction only for rDock (Holm $p = 0.010$) in this smaller set. One effect differed: the RDKit start conformer helped more in complexes without cofactors (Vina +9.2 points [2.7, 15.6], Smina +8.2 [1.8, 14.4], against +4.4 and +3.3 on all 428), an exploratory observation that this design cannot explain.

sentence: The 33 complexes whose Vina outcome changed with the seed alone were strongly over-represented among each arm's flips (odds ratios [[10.5]] – 37; Holm $p < 10^{-8}$ for every arm): with the 2 box, 58\% of them flipped against 9\% of the other complexes.
paragraph: Part of every arm's effect falls on complexes that are unstable anyway. The 33 complexes whose Vina outcome changed with the seed alone were strongly over-represented among each arm's flips (odds ratios 10.5 – 37; Holm $p < 10^{-8}$ for every arm): with the 2 box, 58\% of them flipped against 9\% of the other complexes. But they account for a minority of most arms' flips (Table~ ). The RDKit start conformer changed the outcome of 63 complexes that never changed with the seed, the 2 box 34 and protonation 24. These complexes did not change across four seeds, so most of these flips are likely effects of the preparation choice itself, although four replicates cannot rule out that some of them have a small chance of flipping by chance.

sentence: The one association that survived correction was with the 2 box for Smina, whose flips concentrated on more flexible ligands: a median of 10 rotatable bonds against 6 (rank-biserial $r = [[0.31]]$, Holm $p = 0.001$).
paragraph: Ligand properties explained little. The one association that survived correction was with the 2 box for Smina, whose flips concentrated on more flexible ligands: a median of 10 rotatable bonds against 6 (rank-biserial $r = 0.31$, Holm $p = 0.001$). Vina showed the same tendency without reaching significance (median 29 heavy atoms against 24, $r = 0.21$, Holm $p = 0.057$). Protonation flips leaned towards ligands whose charge it changed for the three Vina-family engines (Vina: 80\% of flipped against 62\% of unflipped complexes, odds ratio 2.5, $p = 0.024$; Gnina 1.7; Smina 1.6) but not for rDock (0.87), and no engine's association survived correction (Holm $p \ge 0.12$). Flips from the RDKit conformer showed no association with ligand size or flexibility in any engine, and no arm's flips were associated with the presence of a cofactor. All but 10 of the supplied ligands are neutral, so the formal charge of the supplied ligand itself could not be tested meaningfully.

sentence: econd, the box was sized to the ligand rather than padded around it: a cube [[2.857]] times the radius of gyration of the docked conformer, centred on the crystal ligand, the optimum found for Vina.
paragraph: Second, the box was sized to the ligand rather than padded around it: a cube 2.857 times the radius of gyration of the docked conformer, centred on the crystal ligand, the optimum found for Vina. These boxes were smaller than the baseline box for 427 complexes (median volume 0.31 times) and smaller than the 2 box for 331 (0.75 times), and for 207 complexes part of the crystal ligand lay outside the box. Success was 50.2\% [45.5, 54.9], above the baseline (+4.0 points; 46 gained, 29 lost; exact McNemar $p = 0.064$) but not above the 2 box (53.0\%; $p = 0.21$). The result split cleanly on whether the crystal ligand fitted (an exploratory, post hoc split): for the 221 complexes whose crystal ligand lay wholly inside the box, success rose from 51.6\% to 59.7\% (22 gained, 4 lost), while for the 207 where it did not, success was unchanged (40.6\% and 40.1\%; 24 gained, 25 lost). A box scaled to the ligand works well when it contains the binding mode, and the gain is lost where the rule truncates it; a small fixed padding around the reference ligand avoids that failure.

paragraph: The sensitivity above can also be used. For each engine and complex, the baseline top-1 pose was compared with the top-1 pose of each of the five primary arms, and the number of arms whose pose lay within 2 of it (0 – 5; a missing pose counts as disagreement) was tested as a predictor of whether the baseline pose was correct (Figure~ ). When all five arms agreed, the baseline pose was correct for 83.7\% [77.4, 88.6] of 166 complexes with Vina, 81.3\% [74.8, 86.4] of 171 with Smina, 92.8\% [88.3, 95.7] of 194 with Gnina and 91.1\% [79.3, 96.5] of 45 with rDock. When none agreed, it was correct for at most 5.6\% (Vina, 2 of 36).

Averaged over every pair of arms, agreement gave an AUROC of 0.775 for Vina, 0.744 for Smina, 0.801 for Gnina and 0.836 for rDock, against 0.857, 0.830, 0.863 and 0.897 with all five arms; a single arm gave 0.67 to 0.76. The same pair, the 2 box with the RDKit start conformer, was the best of the ten for all four engines (0.828, 0.810, 0.828 and 0.894), within 0.03 to 0.05 of all five arms. It was selected on these data, so its advantage over the average pair is optimistic, but that one pair came first for every engine suggests the choice is not arbitrary: it combines a change of search space with a change of starting point.

sentence: Under cross-validation, the agreement levels learned on training folds ranked held-out poses with an AUROC of [[0.838]] for Vina, 0.809 for Smina, 0.835 for Gnina and 0.884 for rDock, against 0.637 to 0.717 for the docking score, and with lower Brier scores (0.118 to 0.162 against 0.201 to 0.234).
paragraph: Because the signal was found on these complexes, it was also evaluated out of sample (Table~ ). Under cross-validation, the agreement levels learned on training folds ranked held-out poses with an AUROC of 0.838 for Vina, 0.809 for Smina, 0.835 for Gnina and 0.884 for rDock, against 0.637 to 0.717 for the docking score, and with lower Brier scores (0.118 to 0.162 against 0.201 to 0.234). Agreement added to the score rather than restating it: a model with both reached held-out AUROCs of 0.857 to 0.906, and adding agreement to the score improved the fit for every engine (likelihood-ratio test, $p < 10^{-30}$). Choosing the best pair of arms inside each training fold, which removes the optimism of choosing it on all the data, gave held-out AUROCs of 0.790 to 0.871, about 0.02 below the in-sample values above. Missing poses do not drive the signal: only 16 Vina and 2 rDock complexes had a missing arm pose, and without them Vina's AUROC was 0.847 instead of 0.857. All of this remains within one dataset; Section~ tests it on another.

Under cross-validation, the agreement levels learned on training folds ranked held-out poses with an AUROC of 0.838 for Vina, 0.809 for Smina, 0.835 for Gnina and 0.884 for rDock, against 0.637 to 0.717 for the docking score, and with lower Brier scores (0.118 to 0.162 against 0.201 to 0.234). Agreement added to the score rather than restating it: a model with both reached held-out AUROCs of 0.857 to 0.906, and adding agreement to the score improved the fit for every engine (likelihood-ratio test, $p < 10^{-30}$). Choosing the best pair of arms inside each training fold, which removes the optimism of choosing it on all the data, gave held-out AUROCs of 0.790 to 0.871, about 0.02 below the in-sample values above. Missing poses do not drive the signal: only 16 Vina and 2 rDock complexes had a missing arm pose, and without them Vina's AUROC was 0.847 instead of 0.857. All of this remains within one dataset; Section~ tests it on another.

sentence: Taking, among the six top-1 poses (baseline and five arms), the one that most of the others agree with (ties keep the baseline pose) changed the chosen pose for [[7.9]]\% (Vina) to 18.2\% (Gnina, rDock) of complexes and raised top-1 success for every engine: Vina from 46.3\% to 48.1\% (11 gained, 3 lost), Smina from 47.0\% to 48.6\% (8 gained, 1 lost), Gnina from 62.6\% to 65.7\% (19 gained, 6 lost) and rDock from 29.4\% to 31.3\% (14 gained, 6 lost).
paragraph: Agreement can also choose the pose. Taking, among the six top-1 poses (baseline and five arms), the one that most of the others agree with (ties keep the baseline pose) changed the chosen pose for 7.9\% (Vina) to 18.2\% (Gnina, rDock) of complexes and raised top-1 success for every engine: Vina from 46.3\% to 48.1\% (11 gained, 3 lost), Smina from 47.0\% to 48.6\% (8 gained, 1 lost), Gnina from 62.6\% to 65.7\% (19 gained, 6 lost) and rDock from 29.4\% to 31.3\% (14 gained, 6 lost). PB-valid success moved the same way. The direction was consistent, but no single engine's gain survived correction over the four engines (Holm $p \ge 0.059$), so the consensus pose is a modest, unconfirmed improvement, whereas agreement as a confidence signal is a large one. As tested, both used six runs per complex, although the confidence signal keeps most of its value with three.
